questions_asked:
When passengers board a commercial flight, what fraction of the seated passengers
typically check at least one bag? Give a rough share, not a precise figure.

At a busy airport screening hall, when one device is down for maintenance, do
operators simply slow down the whole line, or do they keep other units running
at full speed? Which happens in practice?

When a baggage scanner needs a routine maintenance check, is the whole peak
hour disrupted, or is that work done off-peak or staggered among the machines?
expert_answers: Roughly half to two-thirds of seated passengers typically check at least one bag on a commercial flight. This varies widely by route type and carrier: on domestic leisure routes it tends to run higher (often 50–70%), while on short-haul business-heavy or low-cost-carrier routes it can be lower (30–50%). For modeling purposes, a reasonable central estimate is about 50–60% of seated passengers checking at least one bag. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure.

In practice, operators keep the remaining units running at full speed and absorb the outage by letting queues build and wait times grow — they do not deliberately throttle the working machines to a slower uniform pace. Screening lines are parallel-server systems, so throughput is set by the number of functioning units, not by a synchronized line speed.

The practical consequences: the line does not "slow down" as a coordinated action; instead the effective capacity drops by roughly the fraction of units down, queues lengthen, and if the outage is long enough, bags are held or diverted to other lines. Operators may also pull staff to feed the working units faster, but they do not run them below their rated rate.

Routine maintenance is normally scheduled off-peak or staggered among machines, not done during the peak hour. EDS/ETD units are typically taken out of service during low-traffic periods (early morning, late evening, overnight) or one unit at a time so the remaining units cover the load. During the peak hour itself, the realistic disruption is unplanned breakdowns, not routine maintenance — which is why models treat availability as a random ~92% (EDS) / ~98% (ETD) uptime rather than assuming a scheduled peak-hour outage. This is standard operational practice, not a precise figure.
